newsitem.title: INDIA: Russia says trade with India to rise sharply.
newsitem.headline: Russia says trade with India to rise sharply.

text.p: Trade between India and Russia, a victim of the breakup of the Soviet Union, is gathering pace and is projected to more than double by the turn of the century, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Davydov said on Tuesday.
Trade between the former Soviet Union and its Cold War ally India stood at $5.5 billion in 1990, just before the end of the Soviet Union.
But trade flows, undermined by upheaval in Russia, dried up to a mere $1.1 billion in 1993.

"It is not a secret that recently we encountered a long chain of negative events when due to well known reasons the previously existed connections in economy, science and other fields were torn apart," Davydov told a business conference in New Delhi.
"Now we can say that the situation is improving," said Davydov, who is also foreign trade minister.
"The turnover in 1995 came up to $1.9 billion. And we expect that in the current year it will be $2.6 billion."
Davydov said he was confident that trade would touch $6 billion by 2000 and $10 billion by 2005.
Russia accounts for 70 percent of India's trade with the Commonweath of Independent States (CIS), which stood at $2.16 billion in India's 1995/96 fiscal year ending on March 31.

In the Cold War years, India enjoyed a special trade facility which allowed it to use the rupee -- not a "hard", or convertible, currency -- to pay for Soviet goods. The Soviet Union was India's main arms supplier and a major steel partner.
Russia's long road to privatisation, slack import demand and financial uncertainties initially discouraged Indian exports of tea, rice, tobacco and spices, which had been the staple of trade.

"Narrowness of the range of trade items, consisting mainly of raw materials and agricultural goods, should be eliminated," Davydov said. "It is necessary to include in our turnover more high science and high technological goods."
During a visit by Russian President Boris Yeltsin in 1993, New Delhi and Moscow worked out a formula for India to pay back $10 billion in rupee-denominated debt accumulated during the Cold War.

India agreed to pay back the debt by providing $1 billion worth of goods every year. But critics in India said the scheme allowed Russia to pay far less for the goods than it would on the open market.

Former Indian foreign minister Pranab Mukherjee told the conference that India needed to speed up the implemention of a tentative agreement providing for Russian investments in India to cover 10 percent of Delhi's $1 billion annual debt repayment.
